FEASIBILITY & SCOPE

Software System Design Assignment

Topic: Edge-Based Distributed Rate Limiting Middleware

1. Case Study Problem

Modern AI platforms expose multiple services—authentication, chat, billing, and autonomous agents—through APIs. These endpoints may receive frequent requests for login, chat generation, agent execution, document processing, image analysis, and other resource-intensive operations. Excessive or automated traffic can consume compute resources, increase latency, exhaust third-party AI quotas, and affect normal users.

A rate limiter placed only inside a downstream service may reject a request after it has already reached that service. In a distributed microservice environment, independently running instances must also enforce limits consistently. Therefore, CortexAI can benefit from an edge-based distributed rate-limiting layer that evaluates requests early, shares quota state across instances, and protects backend services from excessive traffic.

2. Our Solution – CortexAI

CortexAI is a modular AI platform built around a React and Vite frontend and a Node.js/Express microservice backend. It includes separate Auth, Billing, Chat, and Agent services, with Redis used for shared caching and rate-limit state. The Agent service routes requests to specialized capabilities such as chat, coding, PDF, PPT, image, and search workflows.

For this Software System Design assignment, CortexAI will be used as the base application for designing and evaluating Edge-Based Distributed Rate Limiting Middleware. The proposed enhancement places rate-limit checks at the gateway/edge layer before requests are forwarded to downstream services, while retaining configurable per-user and per-agent policies.

How CortexAI Uses Edge-Based Distributed Rate Limiting Middleware

The design centers on the following concepts:

•Edge request handling: Gateway middleware evaluates incoming requests before proxying them to backend services.

•In-memory key-value state: Redis stores fast-changing counters, expiry information, and shared rate-limit state.

•Sliding-window/token-bucket policy: The design can use a sliding-window counter or token bucket to enforce time-based quotas and controlled bursts. The final algorithm should be selected and documented consistently.

•Distributed synchronization: Multiple gateway instances share quota state through Redis. If local edge counters and batched synchronization are introduced, the design must account for temporary quota overshoot and synchronization delay.

•Policy-based limits: Limits can vary by authenticated user, route, service, or agent type.

•Early rejection: Requests exceeding their quota receive HTTP 429 before consuming downstream application resources, where the gateway can enforce the policy.

3. Scope of the Project

The project focuses on protecting CortexAI's microservices from excessive API traffic while demonstrating distributed rate limiting as a core system-design component.

3.1 Request Interception at the Gateway

Incoming API requests will pass through the gateway middleware. After authentication or trusted identity resolution, the middleware will identify the applicable policy and evaluate the request before forwarding it.

3.2 User and Agent Identification

Rate-limit keys will be based on a trusted user identity and, where relevant, the target service or agent type. IP-based limits may be added as a secondary safeguard. Client-supplied identity headers must not be trusted unless they are overwritten or validated by the gateway.

3.3 Configurable Rate-Limit Policies

The existing Agent service configuration lists the following nominal limits. These are the initial policy values to verify and preserve or revise during implementation.

Additional policies can be defined for authentication, room-like/session operations if introduced, billing endpoints, or other expensive routes. Policy values should be configurable rather than scattered across handlers.

3.4 Rate-Limiting Algorithm

The current Agent limiter uses a Redis fixed-window counter with INCR, EXPIRE, and TTL. The proposed middleware will evaluate whether to retain fixed windows or move to a sliding-window counter or token-bucket design. A token bucket supports controlled bursts; a sliding-window approach provides smoother enforcement over time. The final implementation and report should name the algorithm actually implemented and describe its trade-offs.

3.5 Distributed State and Synchronization

Redis will provide shared rate-limit state for multiple gateway instances. Atomic operations, such as a Redis Lua script or equivalent atomic primitive, should be used to avoid inconsistencies between incrementing a counter and setting its expiry. If local edge counters are periodically synchronized in batches, the report must explain the trade-off between lower coordination overhead and temporary inconsistency or quota overshoot.

3.6 Rate-Limit Responses

When a request exceeds its policy, the middleware will return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a clear error message and, where applicable, Retry-After and remaining-quota information. The response should be consistent across services instead of allowing rate-limit errors to become ordinary HTTP 200 responses.

3.7 Redis Failure Handling

The system will define how the gateway behaves when Redis is unavailable or slow. For resource-intensive operations, a fail-closed policy may protect the platform at the cost of availability; a fail-open policy may preserve access but weaken protection. The selected behavior should be configurable or explicitly justified.

3.8 Monitoring and Logging

A basic monitoring view or structured logs can report:

•Total allowed and rejected requests

•Rate-limit events by route, service, and policy

•Gateway/edge instance identifiers

•Redis errors and latency

•Synchronization batches and synchronization delay, if batching is implemented

•Request latency before and after enabling rate limiting

3.9 Testing and Evaluation

Testing will cover normal traffic, quota boundaries, burst traffic, concurrent requests, multiple gateway instances, expiry behavior, Redis failures, and consistent HTTP 429 responses. Performance claims will be based on measured results rather than assumed values.

4. Technology Stack

5. Out of Scope

•Rebuilding the entire CortexAI application or replacing its existing frontend

•Implementing every planned AI feature, payment integration, or third-party model integration

•Designing a full enterprise-grade API management platform

•Guaranteeing globally strict quotas while using approximate asynchronous synchronization without coordination

•Large-scale production multi-region infrastructure unless explicitly required

•Claiming performance improvements without repeatable measurements

7. Feasibility

7.1 Technical Feasibility

The existing Node.js/Express gateway and Redis integration provide a practical foundation. Middleware can be implemented without redesigning the entire microservice architecture. Distributed correctness depends on atomic state updates, trusted identity, and the chosen synchronization strategy.

7.2 Economic Feasibility

The design can begin with the project's existing technologies and a local Redis instance, keeping prototype costs low. Production edge workers, managed Redis, logging, and load testing may introduce usage-based costs.

7.3 Operational Feasibility

A configurable middleware layer can be maintained alongside the existing services. Centralized policy definitions, consistent error responses, and automated tests should reduce duplicated rate-limit logic and simplify debugging.

8. Conclusion

CortexAI provides a suitable real-world foundation for studying Edge-Based Distributed Rate Limiting Middleware because it contains multiple Express services, a gateway, Redis integration, and existing agent-specific request limits. The proposed enhancement moves quota enforcement closer to the entry point, shares rate-limit state across gateway instances, and standardizes rejection and monitoring behavior. The design will evaluate sliding-window and token-bucket policies and clearly document the consistency trade-offs of any batched synchronization. Testing and measured results will establish whether the middleware improves protection and request-handling behavior.
